Quick guide to picking a model:
â¢ Predicting a number? Linear regression fits a line by minimizing squared errors.
â¢ Need class probabilities? Logistic regression maps a score into (0, 1).
â¢ Irregular local patterns? K-nearest neighbors votes across the k closest points.
â¢ Clear class gap in high dimensions? SVM maximizes the margin between classes.
â¢ Want readable if-then rules? A decision tree splits features into purer leaves.
â¢ Single tree too noisy? Random forest votes across randomized bootstrap trees.
â¢ Chasing strong tabular accuracy? Gradient boosting (like XGBoost) adds shallow trees to fix remaining errors.

ARIMA uses a time seriesâs past to forecast what comes next. ð

Its full name is autoregressive integrated moving average. The three parts work together:
â¢ Integrated: differences between consecutive observations can help create a stationary series.
â¢ Autoregressive: earlier values help predict the next value. After differencing, these are earlier changes.
â¢ Moving average: past forecast errors can shift the next forecast. This is different from averaging recent sales.

In the bakery example, 100, 110 and 118 loaves become changes of 10 and 8. If the next predicted change is 6, the sales forecast becomes 124 loaves.

The settings p, d and q describe the modelâs structure. Its numerical weights are learned from historical data, then predictions are checked on later observations.

â ï¸ Watch out for:
â¢ Uncertainty further ahead
â¢ Weekly repetition may need SARIMA
â¢ Sudden disruptions to historical patterns

What is statistical arbitrage? It's a bet that two similar stocks will move back together, so it works whether the market goes up or down.

1. Find the hedge ratio. In our simulation, when B moves a dollar, A moves about $1.14. That's beta.

2. Track the spread: A minus 1.14 Ã B. Most days it stays close to its average.

3. Turn the spread into a z-score: how many standard deviations it sits from its average.

4. The rule. Above +2, sell A and buy B. Below â2, buy A and sell B. Close the trade when the z-score comes back to 0.

5. Over 250 simulated trading days, the rule triggered 7 trades and all 7 were profitable. The simulation had no trading costs, and the relationship never broke.

6. Real edges are small, so funds run hundreds of pairs at once. In our run, 28 of 30 pairs ended up ahead.

7. The real danger is a pair that stops moving together. The spread never comes back, so every position needs a stop loss.

This is part 5 of Quant From Scratch. Follow for part 6.

What separates candidates in a data science interview case study or past project deep dive: justifying the choices you make when the interviewer pushes back.

Marketplace roles are the clearest example. Many candidates have memorized the pattern that interference creates bias, so you run a geo-based experiment or a switchback; that answer is correct, but it falls apart when the interviewer asks why you chose that design or whether a different approach could work.

Alpha is another place this shows up: saying a result is significant because p < 0.05 just restates the definition. A stronger answer explains why that threshold fits this decision, given the cost of a false positive versus the cost of missing a real effect.

Guardrail metrics are the third. Latency and app crashes matter, but theyâre closer to engineering concerns, and youâll stand out more as a data scientist by picking guardrails tied to the treatment itself, with a clear reason each one could move.

Memorizing the standard pattern is a reasonable starting point, but the candidates who stand out are the ones who can defend each choice under pushback.

Rat Race (2001) is a slapstick ensemble comedy directed by Jerry Zucker and written by Andy Breckman, loosely inspired by the 1963 classic *Itâs a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World*. The plot centers on eccentric Las Vegas casino owner Donald Sinclair (John Cleese), who invents a high-stakes game for his wealthy high-roller friends: six special tokens are planted in slot machines, and the lucky winners are each given a key to a locker in Silver City, New Mexico, containing a duffel bag with $2 million. The first team to reach the locker claims the prize, with no rules limiting how they get there, while Sinclairâs patrons bet on the outcome. This setup launches a chaotic cross-desert race filled with sabotage, mistaken identities, and absurd mishaps.

The competitors form an eccentric ensemble that drives the filmâs frantic energy: narcoleptic Italian tourist Enrico Pollini (Rowan Atkinson), disgraced football referee Owen Templeton (Cuba Gooding Jr.), reunited mother-and-daughter team Vera and Merrill (Whoopi Goldberg and Lanei Chapman), scheming brothers Duane and Blaine (Seth Green and Vince Vieluf), opportunistic tourist father Randy Pear and his family (Jon Lovitz and Kathy Najimy), and strait-laced lawyer Nick Schaffer (Breckin Meyer, paired with helicopter pilot Tracy played by Amy Smart). As they race roughly 560 miles southeast, the groups endure separate but interlocking disastersâfrom stolen vehicles and radar sabotage to hot-air balloons and unexpected celebrity encountersâculminating in a charity concert twist that redirects the prize money. The movie received mixed reviews upon its August 2001 release but performed solidly at the box office and has since gained a following for its broad physical comedy and star-studded cast.

5 minutes of prep, for one of the best healthy meals youâve ever made at home.

Trust me, I get it. I want my food to be exciting, healthy, and keep me ridiculously full. Iâve lost over 155lbs eating meals like this. This is one of those meals thats easy, takes practically no technique, and you can do it all in 1 pot with less than 5 minutes of prep.

Sure, you can sear the chuck roast before putting it in the pot, but this is just as good!

âComment FLAVOR and I will send you how to preorder my new high protein cookbook!

Here is how to make it:

1.Grab an oven safe dish. One with a lid.

2.Place 2lbs of chuck roast at the base. Season it on both sides with salt and pepper. Be generous with the salt. Add 1 tbsp thyme, 1-2 tbsp smoked paprika, and 1/4 to 1/2 tsp cayenne pepper depending on how spicy you want things. Toss in 1 shallot (or half a red onion), 4-6 garlic cloves. And pour in 24oz of bone broth.

3.Cover, pop in the oven at 350F for 3 hours with the lid on.

4.While thats going, cut up whatever root vegetables you like. You can use 3/4lb baby potatoes and 4 medium carrots like I did, or use broccoli, cauliflower, zucchini, celery root, or even Brussel sprouts.

5.Remove the chuck roast from the oven, shred it using 2 forks, toss in your vegetables, put the lid on and put it back in the oven at 400F for 45 minutes.

6.Remove, top with fresh parsley, then eat as is, or alongside some salad, maybe some rice or my kaizen high protein lowcarb rice, quinoa, or whatever youâre craving.

This is such an easy recipe, such a perfect healthy dinner, and one of those fall recipes that is so good.

Chuck Roast Kalbi ð¥ðð¤ 

Today I am letting you in on a local Hawaii secret â using thin-sliced chuck roast for boneless kalbi.

Short rib can get expensive, but chuck roast gives you that same sweet, salty, umami-packed kalbi flavor for way cheaper. Itâs more cost-effective, easy to cook, and perfect for meal prep all week.

I get a lot of questions on if it is dry but trust me, if itâs thinly sliced and cooked right, itâs just as tender as kalbi and still packed full of umami and that beautiful char. And donât sleep on this homemade kalbi marinade! Itâs sweet, savory, and packed with flavor.

Recipe

Ingredients

* Thin-sliced chuck roast that you can get from Costco
* 1 cup brown sugar
* 1 cup shoyu (soy sauce)
* Â¼ cup crushed or grated Asian pear
* Crushed fresh ginger, to taste
* 2 tablespoons sesame oil
* 2 tablespoons rice vinegar

Knife: @montanaknifecompany 
Charcoal: @cowboycharcoal 

Instructions

1. In a mixing bowl, combine the brown sugar, shoyu, Asian pear, crushed ginger, sesame oil, and rice vinegar. Mix until everything is well combined and the sugar dissolves.
2. Pour the marinade over your thin-sliced chuck roast, making sure every piece is evenly coated. Marinate overnight or for at least 30 minutes. I added in extra 1/4 cup of minced jarlic NOT brown sugar.
3. Fire up your grill nice and hot.
4. Grill both sides until you get that beautiful char and caramelization.
5. Top with green onions, sesame seeds, and serve with a side of mac salad and rice.
6. Pack up your leftovers for your weekly meals.

This is a budget-friendly boneless kalbi hack that still brings all the Hawaii plate lunch flavor.

Pure Python questions still show up in data science technical rounds, even though almost nobody writes a groupby by hand on the job. I worked through problems like this one before passing a similar round at Netflix.

The setup: you get a list of dictionaries, each with a studentâs name, grade, and subject, and you need a function that returns the top-scoring student for each subject without using pandas or numpy.

The approach: loop through the list once and keep a plain dictionary that stores the best grade and student name seen so far for each subject. When a new record beats the current max for its subject, you overwrite it, and by the end of the loop you have your answer in a single pass.

Interviewers use this to check whether you understand what pandas is doing under the hood, since a groupby followed by idxmax is really just this loop with a nicer interface. If youâve only ever worked through the library, itâs worth practicing a few of these from scratch before your next technical screen.

A group of aliens decides to test humanityâs potential by granting one ordinary person unlimited power. The person they choose is Neil Clarke â a school teacher with no particular history of consequential decision-making. The test begins.

Absolutely Anything (2015) takes a premise that philosophy has been debating for centuries â what would a person actually do with unlimited power â and answers it with the specific honesty that comedy is uniquely positioned to deliver. Neil doesnât immediately set out to solve world hunger or reverse climate change. 1. Context beats clever prompts: Build context once, then connect the source data.

A maintained project brief or AGENTS.md saves me more time than endlessly rewriting the perfect prompt. I also use permissioned connectors to pull the real source material from email, Google Drive, and my calendar. That way, the agent works from the actual history instead of whatever I remember to paste into chat. That is the idea behind liferepo and GeorgeTeamAgentTemplate.

2. Turn friction into skills: Do the messy version before automating it.

I do not create a skill just because a task might repeat. I run the ugly manual version, note where the agent struggles, and then package the stable workflow. Most of georgeskills came from real annoyances, not from guessing what might be reusable.

3. Ask for receipts, not âdoneâ: Every task should return proof.

Tests, screenshots, source links, or an inspectable diff. In my private george-agents system, âdoneâ is still just a claim until the worker returns an artifact the parent agent can verify.

4. Review becomes the bottleneck: Separate building from judging.

AI makes producing drafts cheap. Deciding what is correct and worth keeping becomes the actual work. I now separate the builder, the evaluator, and the parent agent that decides what survives. The agent that did the work should not be the only agent grading it.

5. Give every agent a stop condition: Define success before it starts.

Without a definition of done, an agent will happily spend another hour polishing the wrong thing. In GeorgeLoops, every recurring workflow needs bounded inputs, an output, a verifier, and an approval gate before it earns automation.

For the Chicken:

-Seasoning: 1 tbsp paprika, 1 tbsp cumin, 1 tbsp onion powder, 2 tsp coriander, 1 tsp allspice, 2 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp pepper, 1 tsp salt
-3 tbsp olive oil + 8 garlic cloves
-Â½ lemon, juiced
-2 tsp @betterthanbouillon roasted chicken base

For the Rice:
-3 tbsp butter + 1 Â½ cups yellow onion, diced
-1 tbsp turmeric, 2 tsp paprika, 2 tsp garlic powder, 2 tsp pepper
-1 Â½ cups basmati rice
-3 cups hot water 
-3 tsp @betterthanbouillon roasted chicken base 

For the Fresh Sumac Salad:
-Â½ large red onion, thinly sliced
-1 cup cherry tomatoes, quartered
-1 cup cucumber, sliced then halved
-1 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper & 2 tsp sumac
-Â½ lemon, juiced

-Â¼ cup mayonnaise + Â¼ cup plain Greek yogurt

Pandas is not slow. Your code is. Hereâs whatâs secretly killing your performance. ð

1ï¸â£ Youâre Using .apply() on a DataFrame

ð This is the #1 Pandas mistake. .apply() is just a slow for-loop in disguise. Replace it with vectorized operations. Example: Instead of df.apply(lambda x: x[âAâ] + x[âBâ], axis=1), use df[âAâ] + df[âBâ]. 100x faster, same result.

2ï¸â£ Youâre Growing a DataFrame in a Loop

ð Never use pd.concat() or .append() inside a loop. Every iteration copies the entire DataFrame. Instead, collect rows in a list, then create the DataFrame once at the end using pd.DataFrame(list). This alone can save you minutes.

3ï¸â£ You Loaded All Columns

ð Donât do pd.read_csv(âhuge_file.csvâ) blindly. Use the usecols parameter to load only what you need. If you only need 3 out of 50 columns, you just cut your memory usage and load time by 90%.

4ï¸â£ Youâre Not Using Categorical Types

ð If you have a column with repeated string values (like âMaleâ/âFemaleâ or country names), convert it to category type using .astype(âcategoryâ). This reduces memory by 10x and speeds up groupby operations massively
